summary: People of Caribbean origin are a formative component to the success and definition of both Toronto and Canada. Today, more than 315,000 Torontonians of Caribbean heritage contribute immensely to the city’s economic, social, political, and cultural composition. One of the largest festivals in Canada, the historic Toronto Caribbean Carnival has grown into North America’s largest Caribbean events. With close to sixty years of bringing Caribbean vibrancy to Toronto’s downtown core, this marquee event draws more than 2 million visitors annually, injecting between $467 million and $532 million into the local economy while cementing itself as a vital piece of Toronto's cultural identity. It is also the pillar of several affiliate events throughout the summer that demonstrate the strength of Toronto’s Caribbean community. Caribbean-owned businesses have driven local economic growth for decades, anchoring prominent cultural hubs like Little Jamaica along Eglinton Avenue West, as well as neighborhoods across Scarborough and the city. At the same time, Caribbean Canadians enrich the broader community as entrepreneurs and essential workers across every major industry, sector, and professional level in Toronto. This impact is especially profound in Scarborough, which is home to approximately 90,000 residents of Caribbean origin. As a major hub for Caribbean commerce, authentic restaurants,…
decided: City Council on July 29 and 30, 2026, adopted the following: 1. City Council proclaim July as Caribbean Heritage Month for the City of Toronto in 2026, and for future years. 2. City Council request the Province of Ontario to proclaim July as Caribbean Heritage Month for the Province for future years. 3. City Council request the Government of Canada to proclaim July as Caribbean Heritage Month for the country for future years.
